extracted.intended_audience: general readers and webcomic creators interested in remixing comics / Garfield fans
extracted.subtask_description: Creating a remix webcomic by editing existing Garfield newspaper strips to remove Garfield (and sometimes other characters) so Jon Arbuckle's lines read as isolated, often existential or bleak humor. Focuses on selection, minimal editing, presentation, and rights/attribution considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of Garfield and thought bubbles (no other changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Garfield Minus Garfield is made from existing Garfield strips, which are edited to remove Garfield the cat and his thought bubbles from the image, as well as removing other characters such as Nermal and Odie. No other changes are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only permitted edits are deletions of Garfield (and sometimes other characters/thought balloons); do not otherwise redraw, rewrite, or alter panels. This preservation of the original art except for removals produces the effect of Jon talking to himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select strips that make Jon seem 'metaphysically tormented'
rubrics_metrics.description: Walsh said that he deliberately chose strips that would make Jon seem as 'metaphysically tormented' as possible, saying 'If Jon is happy, my strips don't work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing source strips, prioritize panels where Jon's dialogue or posture, when isolated, suggests existential crisis, despair, or neurosis. Avoid strips where Jon appears happy or neutral because the recontextualized effect depends on melancholic/awkward material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for existential/bleak tone rather than punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the cutesy thought-bubbles of his lasagna-loving cat, Jon's observations seem to teeter between existential crisis and deep despair; reviewers compared the result to Samuel Beckett and bleak early Peanuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The creative goal is to surface loneliness, neurosis, or bleak humor rather than a conventional joke structure. Select and present strips to emphasize mood and subtext over punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal production time / low-effort editing approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2008, Walsh published a comic each day. Each comic took about five minutes to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process can be fast and low-effort—simple deletions can produce publishable content daily. This suggests a workflow emphasizing quantity and rapid turnaround rather than heavy reworking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation choice: pairing originals with edits can lessen the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A review in the New Yorker said that publishing the original comics next to the edited ones 'vastly lessens the effect of "Minus"' and Paws, Inc.'s version included the original Garfield strip underneath the edited one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If preserving the disorienting/recontextualized effect is important, avoid presenting the original alongside the edit. Including originals may explain away or dilute the reinterpretation, even if done for brand-protection or comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution, approval, and publication by rights-holders
rubrics_metrics.description: Jim Davis, the creator of Garfield, approved of the project, and an official Garfield book (also called Garfield Minus Garfield) was published by his company. The book was credited to Jim Davis with a foreword by Dan Walsh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remix projects intersect with creator/rights-holder interests; securing approval or collaborating with the original rights-holder may affect publication options, crediting, and distribution (and can result in official releases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning within remix/comic-edit traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic followed a number of other remixes of newspaper comic strips, such as The Dysfunctional Family Circus and Marmaduke Explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should be aware of precedents and audience expectations for comic remixes (deletion, recontextualization). Studying similar projects can inform selection, legal/ethical approaches, and stylistic choices.
